rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Newton's law of gravitation: every particle attracts every other with $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$ along the line joining them — proportional to the product of masses, inversely proportional to the **square** of the distance. $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$ N m² kg⁻² is universal (Cavendish torsion balance), unlike the local $g$.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - F = Gm₁m₂/r² - G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² - g = GM/R² (link to weight)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Universal Scope:** Newton's law ($F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$) applies to *all* masses in the universe, at all distances. It is exact for point masses or spherically symmetric bodies (Shell Theorem). For non-spherical objects, integration or numerical methods are required.  ·  **Inverse-Square Nature:** The $1/r^2$ dependence means the force has infinite range but drops rapidly. It never reaches zero at any finite distance. This inverse-square law is equivalent to saying gravitational flux through a closed surface is proportional to enclosed mass (Gauss's law for gravity).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Use the centre-to-centre distance in r — for spheres this is the distance between centres.  ·  G is the same everywhere; g is NOT — it varies with location and height.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Two 100 kg spheres 1 m apart*** attract with 6.67×10⁻⁷ N — gravity matters only at planetary scale.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **G vs g:** G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² is universal; g = 9.8 m/s² is Earth-local and varies with location.  ·  **Equal forces, unequal effects:** Earth and you attract each other equally — Earth barely notices because of its huge mass.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Solve 5 numericals using $F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$.  ·  Compute g at the surface and at various heights of a planet.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "2m definition: statement + formula + G's value and meaning."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Short (2m): Two balls of 5 kg each, 0.5 m apart — find the gravitational force.** — F = Gm₁m₂/r² = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ × 25/0.25 = 6.67×10⁻⁹ N — immeasurably small, which is why G was so hard to measure.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: The definition question repeats (2019, 2024) — include the formula and G's units.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **One law, two worlds:** the same F = Gm₁m₂/r² governs falling apples and orbiting moons.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$; G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² (universal, Cavendish).  ·  Always attractive, central, inverse-square, medium-independent, unshieldable.  ·  It obeys Newton's third law — equal and opposite pair forces.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Cavendish's torsion-balance experiment (1798) measured G — and thereby "weighed the Earth".

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — One Law for the Universe An apple falls and the Moon orbits by the same rule. Newton's law of gravitation states that every particle attracts every other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation — the first law that explained both heaven and Earth.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2019, 2024) ### 2.1 Statement **Every particle of matter in the universe attracts every other particle with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.** $$F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$$ directed along the line joining the two particles.…  ·  ## 3. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topic 31:** $g = GM/R^2$ follows by equating $mg = GMm/R^2$. - **To Unit 4 (Newton's laws):** the third-law symmetry verified here. - **To Kepler's laws:** the inverse-square law yields elliptical orbits and $T^2 \propto r^3$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **G vs g Distinction:** $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N·m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ is a *universal constant*. $g = GM/r^2$ is the *local gravitational field strength*, varying with location. On Earth's surface $g \approx 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$; at height $h$, $g' = g(R/(R+h))^2$.  ·  Newton's third law applies to gravity: the forces on the two masses are equal and opposite.  ·  For points above Earth's surface use $g = \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2}$; inside use $g = g(1 - d/R)$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NEB numericals commonly give m₁, m₂, r and ask for F; or ask for g at a height.  ·  Verified PYQs: state law + G (2024, 2m); third-law check (2019, 2m).  ·  "Every particle of matter attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their distance."

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Why doesn't the Sun's pull rip the Moon away from Earth?  ·  Derive the orbital velocity and period formulas from the law.  ·  Compare gravitational and electric forces for the same particles.
